name: Mahesh
definition: Mahesh is a composite portrait of a Kuruba auto-rickshaw driver and small farmer in Kollegal town, Chamarajanagara district, navigating seasonal drought, irregular fares and the costs of sending three children to school. He is drawn from the lived experience of families in this border taluk who balance urban gig work with rainfed farming and hope their children will escape both.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Mahesh owns a thirteen-year-old auto-rickshaw and operates on the Kollegal town stand, ferrying passengers to the taluk hospital, the bus station, nearby villages and occasionally across the Tamil Nadu border to Bargur or Dhimbam. His daily income varies sharply: a good day brings seven hundred rupees, a lean one barely two hundred, with fuel, maintenance and the monthly loan instalment eating into every trip. He also cultivates three acres of dryland on his wife's family's holding, two kilometres outside Kollegal, where he grows ragi and cotton under uncertain rainfall. Ploughing, weeding and harvest pull him away from the auto stand for weeks at a time, forcing him to skip days or leave the vehicle idle while his eldest son, who left PU college after first year, sometimes takes short trips. The cotton crop failed last year after a delayed monsoon, leaving him with a thirteen-thousand-rupee loss and an outstanding pesticide bill. Auto work offers cash flow but no security: fares drop in the monsoon, maintenance costs spike on potholed roads, and competition from app-based bike taxis has begun to cut into his regulars. He wakes at five, checks the farm if it is the season, reaches the stand by seven and works until eight or nine at night, returning home bone-tired to a meal of ragi mudde his wife keeps warm.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Mahesh lives with his wife, three children and his widowed mother in a small house they built twelve years ago on a site his wife inherited at the edge of Kollegal. His wife, forty-two, works as a domestic help in three households in the town, earning four thousand rupees a month; she also manages the farm labour they hire at peak times and cooks, cleans and cares for his seventy-year-old mother, who has diabetes and poor eyesight. Their eldest son, twenty-two, dropped out of first-year PU commerce to help on the farm and occasionally drives the auto; Mahesh had hoped he would finish and find a government job, but the boy saw no point and now talks of migrating to Bengaluru for factory work. Their daughter, eighteen, passed SSLC last year and is in second PU science at the government college in Kollegal; she is bright, wants to study nursing, and Mahesh is determined she will not marry before finishing, though relatives have begun to ask. Their youngest son, fourteen, is in ninth standard at the town high school and shows interest in mechanics. Mahesh's wife makes most day-to-day decisions about the children's schooling and health; he defers to her on household spending but insists on the final word about land and the auto. Gender roles are clear: she manages the inside, he the outside, though the lines blur when cash runs short and both scramble to cover fees or medical bills. His mother's insulin and eye drops cost fifteen hundred a month, a strain they carry without complaint.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Mahesh himself studied only up to seventh standard in a village school before his father pulled him out to work; he regrets it and is fierce that his children will study further. His daughter attends the Government PU College in Kollegal, where the Shakti scheme and a bicycle have made daily travel possible; fees are low, but books, uniforms and the biology practical kit cost money, and private tuition for the CET exam will be another expense he has not yet figured out how to meet. His youngest son goes to the government high school in town, within walking distance, and pays no fees under the guarantee schemes; still, Mahesh spends roughly two thousand rupees a term on notebooks, shoes and the odd teacher's demand for photocopies or charts. Mahesh had dreamed of an office job for him, but the dream died and he does not speak of it now. His daughter's nursing ambition fills that void; if she clears CET, he will mortgage the farm to pay for a private nursing college if no government seat comes. The schools are there, but the jobs the degrees promise feel distant and uncertain, and he wonders if his sacrifice will be enough.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Mahesh's mother's diabetes is the household's chronic worry: her fasting sugar runs high, the government hospital in Kollegal dispenses insulin and metformin free under Arogya Karnataka, but the strips for her glucometer, her diet and the quarterly specialist check-up in Mysuru cost time and money they juggle month to month. Last year she had a hypoglycaemic episode at home and Mahesh rushed her to the taluk hospital; the doctor stabilised her and scolded him for irregular monitoring, a rebuke he felt keenly. His own health he ignores: his knees ache from clutch-work, his back hurts, he has a persistent cough he attributes to dust and exhaust, but he has not seen a doctor in three years because he cannot afford to stop earning. His wife suffers from anaemia—she was prescribed iron tablets at the anganwadi during a check-up for his mother—but takes them irregularly and says she is too busy to rest. The children have been mostly healthy, though his daughter had dengue two years ago and the week in a private Kollegal clinic cost twenty-two thousand rupees, borrowed from a relative and still being repaid. They rely on the government hospital for fevers and injuries, but serious illness means private care, debt and fear. The free-medicine scheme helps, but stocks run out and the pharmacy then quotes prices that sting. Mahesh's main health fear is an accident or major illness that would stop him working; he has no insurance, and a month without income would topple the family. He drinks occasionally, more when the crop fails or fares are lean, and his wife worries but says nothing.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Mahesh is Kuruba, a shepherding community with a presence across Mysuru and Chamarajanagara, though his family left herding two generations ago for farming and town work. He participates in Kuruba Sangha meetings in Kollegal, where men discuss caste-certificate issues, scholarship access for ST/OBC children and, occasionally, politics; he feels pride when the chief minister's Kuruba background is mentioned, though he is sceptical that it has brought tangible benefit to families like his. His wife is also Kuruba, from a village near Yelandur; the marriage was arranged by their parents twenty-three years ago and cost his father a debt that took years to clear. He is a believer but not devout: they keep a picture of Hanuman and a calendar image of Male Mahadeshwara at home, his wife lights a lamp most evenings, and once a year they try to visit the MM Hills temple, a journey that mixes pilgrimage and picnic. He fasts on Ayudha Puja, the one festival he holds to strictly, and joins the Kollegal Dasara procession as a spectator, though the grand Mysuru celebration feels like another world. Socially, he moves mostly among other auto drivers, a mixed group of Kuruba, Vokkaliga, SC and Muslim men; caste matters in marriage and politics, less so at the stand. He resents the Vokkaliga domination of local contracts and taluk offices but does not dwell on it. His closest friends are two other drivers and a mechanic who gives him credit on parts; they drink tea together at the stand, discuss fares, crops, children's marks and the state of the roads, a daily solidarity that sustains him.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Mahesh votes in every election, though he says the results rarely change his life. The taluk panchayat is a distant body; he has never attended a meeting and does not know his member's name. The RTO office he knows too well: auto permits, insurance renewals and the bribes one pays to avoid being fined for a cracked mirror or an expired pollution certificate. He drew a Below Poverty Line card years ago, now reclassified under some new survey he does not fully understand; his family gets the PDS rice and Anna Bhagya ragi, though the ration-shop keeper is often rude and weighs short. He has never tried for MGNREGA work—too many days needed on the farm or the stand—but his wife's brother in a nearby village says it offers a fallback when nothing else does. The government hospital saved his mother's life, the school is free, but every other interaction feels like a battle: forms, certificates, queues, officers who assume he is lying or ignorant. He has heard of the Aspirational District label for Chamarajanagara, though he does not know what it means in practice, and he doubts anyone in Bengaluru thinks much about Kollegal's roads or water or the fact that every auto driver here is one breakdown away from ruin.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Mahesh is proud of his work ethic, his daughter's marks and the fact that he has kept the family fed and housed without begging anyone, but he is haunted by a fear that it is not enough and never will be. He worries most about his daughter's CET exam and the nursing-college fees he does not have; if she fails to get a seat or drops out, he will feel he has failed her. He worries about his eldest son's aimlessness and the temptation of Bengaluru, where he might earn more but also fall into bad company or waste his youth in a factory with no future. He worries about the auto's engine, which makes a new noise, and about the loan instalment due next week. He is angry, quietly, at a system that taxes his fuel, fines his vehicle, ignores his crop loss and offers his children schools with no teachers, then asks what more he wants. He blames no one in particular—not the government, not the rich, not fate—but he feels cheated by a promise that hard work leads somewhere when for him it has led only to the same stand, the same three acres and the same grinding calculations every month. He is proud of his community's recent political prominence, but he does not see it in his life: no road has been paved, no hospital expanded, no auto union given voice. What he wants is simple: his daughter in a nursing uniform, his youngest son in a decent trade, his wife free from other people's kitchens, and himself still able to drive and farm until they no longer need him. He does not expect it to happen, but he will break himself trying, because surrender is not in him.
